a, Correspondence between the GB cell-state annotations used in this study and the GB meta-modules defined by Neftel et al.10. Each malignant cell was scored for every Neftel meta-module by signature scoring on log-normalized RNA (excluding the cell-cycle modules G1/S and G2/M), and assigned to its highest-scoring module. Shown is the proportion of cells in each cell state that map to each Neftel et al. meta-module. b, Cell-state prediction accuracy of the classifier in Fig. 1b, trained on gene expression from a random 80% of 16,423 metacells (9,464 GB, 6,959 TME; 12 patients). Accuracy is shown for the held-out 20% (n = 3,285) using gene expression, and for all metacells using gene accessibility. Cell states are predicted less accurately from accessibility than from expression, most pronounced for malignant states, indicating elevated epigenetic plasticity. c, Uncertainty (entropy) of expression-based cell-state predictions per metacell (n = 16,423 metacells). Low uncertainty across all cell states confirms that expression profiles support confident state assignment. d, Evaluation of cell-state prediction accuracy of the cell-state classifier as in b, however trained on human neurodevelopmental cell types of a multi-ome brain atlas (12 donors; early fetal, late fetal and post-natal stages48), evaluated based on gene expression (held-out 20%; n = 512 metacells) and gene accessibility (n = 2,559 metacells). Cell-state predictions show comparable accuracy across modalities, except in progenitor populations. e, Epigenetic plasticity across neurodevelopmental metacells (n = 2,559), analysed as in Fig. 1c,d. Top: Epigenetic plasticity score (prediction entropy) across the cell types in d. Bottom: Percentage of cells from each expression-defined state (columns) assigned to each state from gene accessibility (rows). Off-diagonal values reflect accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states. As expected, radial glia and NPCs show the highest epigenetic plasticity (P = 7.5 × 10−59, two-sided t-test). f, Schematic of the canonical neurodevelopmental lineage relationships among the cell types analysed in d,e. Radial glia sit at the apex and give rise to three differentiation routes: Towards neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, with plasticity decreasing along each route as cells mature. g, Global correlation between gene expression and accessibility in GB metacells (Pearson r across n = 21,369 genes), stratified by cell state. The concordance of correlation levels across GB cell states suggests that state-specific differences in epigenetic plasticity are not driven by differences in the global coupling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility. h, Average epigenetic plasticity per patient (n = 12) for the cell states in b, computed with the linear model of Fig. 1e after downsampling each state to equal cell numbers. Plasticity trends match those in Fig. 1e, indicating that the observed differences are not driven by variation in cell abundance. i, Average epigenetic plasticity score of GB states (n = 9) across patients. Although individual patients exhibit variation in plasticity across states, the average plasticity is comparable across patients (one-way ANOVA, P = 0.53). j, Donor-associated variation in epigenetic plasticity within defined cell neighbourhoods, shown as the ratio of the standard deviation of mean plasticity scores across donors to the standard deviation across all cells. Values were computed using k = 10 or k = 30 neighbours for each metacell (n = 4,813 and n = 11,868 metacells respectively), considering neighbourhoods represented by at least three donors, and stratified by state. Donor-associated variation was lower than overall local variation in plasticity across all malignant states. Box plots in c,e,g–j show median and IQR, 1.5 × IQR (whiskers), and outliers. Illustration in f created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Two-phase training scheme. Phase 1: Topic construction by joint training of the core autoencoder modules. scDORI embeds paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq profiles in a shared latent Topic space, from which three modules reconstruct the data. Module 1 maps Topic proportions to peak accessibility through a linear decoder with batch-specific adjustments. Module 2 predicts gene expression from the denoised Topic-specific accessibility of Module 1, using a learnable gene–peak linkage matrix restricted to a fixed genomic window around each gene. Module 3 reconstructs TF expression through Topic-TF weights. The three modules are trained jointly, minimizing the sum of their reconstruction losses together with regularization terms. Phase 2: Fine-tuning for eGRN inference. A fourth module infers Topic-specific TF–gene-regulatory links. In silico TF–peak binding scores, signed for activation or repression, are weighted by Topic-specific peak accessibility (Module 1) and propagated to target genes through the gene–peak links (Module 2). Learnable TF–gene-Topic weights adjust these links according to TF–target expression co-variation, and activating and repressive contributions are combined into a net regulatory score that predicts gene expression from Topic-level TF expression (Module 3). The encoder, gene–peak links, and Topic–peak decoder are optionally frozen during fine-tuning, with sparsity constraints on the learned TF–gene weights. b, Training runtime of scDORI as a function of dataset size, shown for Phase 1, Phase 2, and both phases combined, measured on subsampled multi-ome data from the GB atlas. Runtime scales to datasets of millions of cells. Empirical runtimes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU (32 GB). c, Assessment of peak–gene link predictions in three cell lines (IMR90, K562, GM12878) of the published ENCODE dataset76,77, converted to semi-synthetic single-cell multi-ome data as in18 and scored against curated experimentally supported enhancer–gene links from BENGI33 as ground truth. Benchmarks span nine evidence x cell-line combinations available in BENGI, drawn from seven evidence sources derived from chromatin configuration, perturbation, and genomic interaction assays. AUPRC is shown for recovered peak–gene pairs with scDORI and SCENIC+. scDORI achieved higher AUPRC than SCENIC+ in all nine comparisons (P = 2.0 × 10−3, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 9 paired comparisons). Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Average Topic activity in malignant and TME states. Extended version of Fig. 2c showing data for 31 Topics (all Topics with max activation > 0.1 across cells). Key biological functions of each Topic based on GSEA are shown. Raw values and complete pathway analysis are reported in Supplementary Table 2. b, Activity of GB-associated Topics in all cells visualized on the UMAP representation of Fig. 1a. State-specific, inter-state, and pan-state Topics are labelled accordingly. c, Activity of GB-associated Topics across patients. Shown is the number of patients with at least 1% of their cells exhibiting activity (>0.05) for each Topic. All GB Topics are active in at least 4 out of 12 patients, confirming that Topics capture universal regulatory programs of GB.

a, UMAP visualization of ATAC peaks in the patient atlas using Topic–peak scores (from scDORI Module 1) as embedding. (Left) Z-scored accessibility of peaks in each GB state. (Right) Topic–peak score for selected Topics. Topics identify distinct groups of co-accessible peaks within each GB state, reflecting different gene-regulatory programs active in those states. b, Genomic distance distributions between peak–gene pairs inferred by scDORI or MOFA29. For each peak in a MOFA factor, we picked the closest gene that was also part of the same factor. Red lines mark the cis-distance (150 kb) constraint applied to scDORI. Black lines indicate the ±1 Mb assessment window, and interchromosomal peak–gene pairs are shown separately on the left. c, Comparison of cell type prediction in our GB dataset using three latent space embeddings: scDORI (50 Topics), MOFA (50 factors), and SCENIC+ (AUCell-based TF activity scores from 195 TFs). Logistic regression models were trained to predict cell type labels from the latent embeddings of each method, using n = 9,464 GB and n = 6,959 TME metacells as input. scDORI achieved higher mean per-cell type accuracy (88.0%) than MOFA (80.3%; 17/17 cell types, P = 8 × 10−6) and SCENIC+ (85.2%; 11/17 cell types, P = 2.7 × 10−3), with the advantage over SCENIC+ concentrated in malignant states. P-values were obtained from a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. d, Stability of scDORI gene programs across random initializations. Shown is the Jaccard similarity between the top 500 genes of the most active Topic in each GB state, comparing the reference run (Run 0) against three additional runs trained with different random seeds. A randomized version of the reference Topic–gene set serves as a negative control. Gene programs are recovered consistently across runs. e, Activity patterns of selected scDORI Topics derived from our patient atlas projected onto a reference single-cell GB atlas from Neftel et al.10. Colour denotes average Topic activity, and bars on the left show the proportion of cells from each state in our atlas among the top 5,000 cells for each scDORI Topic. The mapping of scDORI Topics to GB cell states is highly concordant across datasets. f, Activity of selected scDORI Topics within malignant cells of the Neftel GB atlas in e, visualized on a UMAP embedding. Neftel state annotations and Leiden-clustered subpopulations are indicated. g, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ eGRNs in predicting DEGs between the Neftel GB cell states shown in e, following the GRaNPA21 framework. For each state pair a logistic regression model was trained to predict whether each gene is up- or downregulated based on the signed TF–gene links in each eGRN. Genes were split into four cross-validation folds, with test genes held out from training. AUPRC is shown for all state pairs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 3.1 × 10−5 for each, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 15 pairs) and perform comparably to each other. h, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ in predicting DEGs between the Leiden clusters shown in f, computed as in g. AUPRC is shown for every cluster pair, considering either scDORI or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 4.4 × 10−19 and P = 4.3 × 10−19, respectively; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 104 pairs).

a, Quality control of the gain-of-function screen described in Fig. 3. Shown are distributions of UMI counts, detected genes, and mitochondrial read fractions, stratified by seeding density (High: 14,000 cells/cm2; low: 9,000 cells/cm2) and biological replicate, separately for each PDGC line (S24, P3XX, and BG5). b, Cells recovered after quality control and barcode demultiplexing. Left: Relative contribution of each cell line, replicate, and seeding density to the total of 261,566 cells. Right: Fraction of cells recovered per TF perturbation, shown for the pooled dataset and for each patient line. TF representation is balanced across lines. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). c, Expression bimodality coefficients (BC) of all screened TFs in OE and control cells from b. Each dot is a TF (n = 55). Violin centre line, median; error bars, extrema. Expression is bimodal (BC > 0.555) for every TF in the OE populations and for 54 of 55 TFs in the controls, reflecting heterogeneous expression of the targeted TFs and motivating exclusion of low- and high TF-expressing cells from respective populations in each OE-versus-control comparison. Inset: ASCL1 expression in control and ASCL1-overexpressing cells. d, Effect of the endogenous-expression filter on control cell heterogeneity in b. Each dot is one TF from the OE screen (n = 55), showing the change in state proportions (left) or in average entropy (right) after removing control cells with high endogenous expression of that TF (above the tenth percentile). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Filtering left state heterogeneity essentially unchanged: change in entropy did not differ from zero (P = 0.14, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 220) and mean changes in individual state proportions were at most 0.025. e, Proportion of cells from each GB state in unperturbed control populations across pooled or individual PDGC lines in b. Total cell counts per condition indicated above. All GB states are, to varying degrees, represented in control cells across all lines. f, Validation of state regulator ranking by scDORI and SCENIC+. For each GB state, the average change in state probability (Δ state score, OE versus control) is shown for the top N predicted regulators of that state, with the average change in the remaining TFs (54 − N) plotted below for comparison. Shaded regions indicate s.d. intervals. Regulators nominated by scDORI induced their predicted state more strongly than those nominated by SCENIC+ (P = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 40 state × N combinations, scDORI higher in 34 of 40), most notably for the neuronal-like and AC-like states. g, Induction of Topic programs after gain-of-function of scDORI-predicted regulators of each Topic. For each top regulator (scDORI regulator score > 0.25), the change in activity of its predicted Topic is shown (Δ Topic score, OE vs. control). Dot size denotes the number of PDGC lines in which the effect was significant (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05) and colour denotes the scDORI regulator score. Regulators of nearly all Topics induced their predicted Topic program. All Topic-level effects per TF are provided in Supplementary Table 3. h, Concordance of Topic- and state-level effects after OE of scDORI-predicted regulators. Each point corresponds to one TF-Topic prediction, positioned by the change it induced in that Topic (x-axis) and in the corresponding state (y-axis), relative to control cells. TFs predicted to regulate several Topics appear once per Topic. Colour denotes the predicted Topic and dot style the significance category (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05). Most regulators induced Topic and state changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Supplementary Table 3). i, Number of DEGs per TF OE condition versus the number of OE cells, per cell line in b. The dashed line depicts a linear regression fit. DEG count scaled positively with the number of OE cells (Spearman r = 0.87, P = 1.9 × 10−50, n = 162 TF × cell-line conditions), reflecting increased statistical power with greater cell coverage. j, Number of upregulated and downregulated genes in TF-overexpressing cells relative to control cells in each PDGC line in b. Bars show the mean ± s.d. of each direction. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). Top 100 DEGs per condition are reported in Supplementary Table 3.

a, Availability of TRs across GB states. Left: Schematic illustrating how a TR can be selectively expressed in its native Topic but epigenetically primed in cells of alternative states. Right: Mean chromatin accessibility (colour intensity) and mean expression (dot size) of indicated TRs across GB Topics. Bars on top indicate availability of TRs in Topics of alternative states, either by expression (scaled expression>0.5; purple) or epigenetic priming (scaled accessibility>0.5, scaled expression<0.3; green). b, Average expression (left) and chromatin accessibility (right) of the top TRs (activity score>0.05) of each target Topic within cells of each source Topic. TR expression is largely confined to Topics of the same GB state, whereas TR accessibility extends broadly to Topics of alternative states, indicating epigenetic priming for future activation. c, TAP between Topic pairs, scaled by the number of expressed TFs in the source Topic and by the weight of self-regulatory links in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). OPC-NPC-like (25, 34) and AC-like (9, 44) tTopics show multiple strong links towards alternative state Topics, whereas links from neuronal-like Topics remain largely within their own state. Full list of TAP scores provided in Supplementary Table 4. d, Changes in TAP scores when using TR accessibility or expression in source Topic for computation. Positive values indicate TAP links mainly influenced by epigenetic priming of TRs, which encompass many of the links between different states. e, Number of top TRs from alternative states (activity score>0.5) that are epigenetically primed in each GB state. The epigenetic priming of alternative state TRs reflects transition potential patterns. f, Variance component analysis of TAP scores across Topic pairs. Each bar shows the proportion of variance explained by a single biological feature, fitted separately in an ordinary least squares model and stratified by whether the target Topic belongs to the same/related state (yellow; n = 77 Topic pairs), an alternative state (orange; n = 212), or any state (purple; n = 289). Regulatory links inferred from the eGRNs explain the largest share of TAP variance. For transitions towards alternative states, epigenetic priming of TRs contributes more than their expression level. g, TRS values between pairs of Topics. Neuronal-like Topics (24, 37) exert the highest repressive effects towards alternative state Topics. Asterisks label significant TRS links, estimated as in c. Full list of TRS values provided in Supplementary Table 4. h, Repression exerted by each source Topic towards the top 50 marker genes from each state identified by the linear model in Fig. 1b, instead of TRs. Similar to TR-level repression, neuronal-like Topics (24, 49) exert the strongest repression towards genes of alternative states. i, Cumulative repression exerted by individual source Topics towards genes of alternative Topics or states. Neuronal-like Topic 24 exerts the strongest repression against alternative identities. j,k, Net transition potential between Topics, as determined by the difference between TAP and TRS values between Topic pairs. Three distinct regulatory mechanisms underlie net transition potential interactions with alternative Topics: (i) predominant repression (Topic 24), (ii) predominant activation (Topics 9 and 34), and (iii) limited activation or repression (Topic 19). Raw values are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of dorsal telencephalon development, depicting neurogenic and gliogenic differentiation trajectories from radial glia towards differentiated neuronal and glial cell types. The shown differentiation hierarchy was reconstructed from available lineage-tracing studies49,50,51. NPC: Neural progenitor cell, OPC: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell, GPC: Glial progenitor cell. b, Activity of selected Topics inferred by scDORI from a developmental brain atlas (n = 12 donors)48. Colour denotes average Topic activity scaled across cell types of dorsal telencephalic origin, collected during early fetal, late fetal, and post-natal development stages. Topic-regulated programs are labelled on the right, determined based on Topic activity patterns, associated genes, and TF regulators. UL: Upper-layer, DL: Deep-layer. Full list of inferred Topics reported in Supplementary Table 5. c, TRs identified in developmental Topics in b recovered canonical lineage regulators, including PAX6 and GLI3 in radial glia114, SOX11 in fetal neurons115, CUX2 in UL neurons116, FOXP2 in DL neurons117, SOX9 in astrocytes118, OLIG1 in OPCs119, and MYRF in oligodendrocytes120, indicating high-confidence prediction of bona fide fate regulators. d, TAP, TRS and net transition potential (TAP–TRS) between pairs of developmental Topics in b. Shown are the respective values scaled by the number of TFs in the source Topic and self-activation in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). Progenitor Topics show broad transition potential toward downstream lineages, whereas terminally differentiated cell type Topics show little or no transition potential towards alternative lineages, often constrained by repression. These results reflect the canonical differentiation hierarchy shown in a, as well as dedifferentiation potentials described for OPCs and astrocytes51,52, demonstrating that our transition model captures biologically coherent relationships. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of the approach used to compute spatial co-activity of Topics across 97 matched tumour sections profiled by Visium spatial transcriptomics. For every section and Topic pair, the pairwise Euclidean distance between Topic A and Topic B spots is computed. Spatial co-activity is defined as the fraction of sections in which the closest 10% of spot pairs are spatially overlapping. Because spatial distance is symmetric by construction, net transition potentials (TAP–TRS) are symmetrized before row-wise Pearson correlation. b, Number of Visium sections and patients represented per Topic pair in the analysis described in a. All Topic pairs were covered by at least 20 sections derived from at least 7 patients, supporting the generalizability of the reported spatial co-activity patterns. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average spatial co-activity between Topic pairs computed as described in a (right), compared to their symmetric net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tend to be spatially co-active, as evidenced by row-wise correlations (Pearson r, right bar). Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of spatial co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 6. d, Schematic of how temporal co-activity of Topics was computed across pseudotime-aligned clonal trajectories. For each Topic pair, we averaged the cosine similarity of their temporal profiles across the top 10% of trajectories in which the two Topics were most temporally proximal, and compared the resulting matrix to net transition potential using column-wise (r1) and row-wise (r2) Pearson correlations, which capture incoming and outgoing transition relationships, respectively. e, Number of clonal populations per patient considered for the temporal analysis in d. A total of 57 clonal trajectories from all 12 patients were considered. f, Average temporal co-activity of Topics as described in d,e compared to net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tended to be temporally co-active for incoming and outgoing transitions, as evidenced by column-wise (top bar) and row-wise (right bar) correlations. Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of temporal co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 7. g, Correlation between Topic spatial co-activity and symmetric net transition potentials associated with each source Topic (n = 17). TAP and TRS values were computed using Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, SCENIC+ eGRNs, or random eGRNs. Dot colour represents the source Topic. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs result in significantly higher correlation with spatial co-activity patterns than those derived using alternative GRNs (P = 0.0057 vs. Union; P = 0.0117 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). h, Same as in g, but correlating temporal co-activity patterns in f and net transition potentials. Values denote the average between column-wise (incoming links, r1) and row-wise (outgoing links, r2) correlations for each Topic. Net transition potential values estimated with Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs positively correlated with temporal co-activity, significantly outperforming those derived from alternative methods (P = 0.0052 vs. Union; P = 0.0026 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). i, Average epigenetic plasticity of cells in each Topic (as in Fig. 1c, top 5,000 cells per Topic) compared with (i) the cumulative net transition potential towards alternative state Topics (Topic-driven plasticity) and (ii) the total repression exerted by each Topic, both computed from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs best recapitulate observed epigenetic plasticity, with modelled plasticity and repression showing significant positive (r = 0.71, P = 0.002) and negative (r = −0.512, P = 0.036) correlations, respectively. Yellow boxes indicate P < 0.05. Box plots in g,h show median and IQR; whiskers are 1.5 × IQR. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Predicted regulatory roles of indicated neuronal-like TFs based on scDORI. Heat map colours indicate differences in the number of activated and repressed marker genes of each Topic (top 250). Dot size and colour denote TF-driven regulation of target TRs (TAP/TRS analysis, Supplementary Table 4). Repressors are predicted to broadly silence non-neuronal-like Topics, while activators selectively induce neuronal-like programs. b, OE levels of neuronal-like TFs in a at day 3 post-transduction in S24 PDGCs, quantified by qPCR, normalized to GFP vector controls (n = 3 independent transductions). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Proportion of scDORI or SCENIC+ predicted target genes showing concordant changes in both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b. PBX1 and SOX4 were excluded because of insufficient changing gene sets (<500). Despite differences in regulon size across methods, the proportion of targets responding to perturbation was comparable. d, Percentage of target gene-regulatory directions accurately (green) or incorrectly (brown) predicted by scDORI or SCENIC+ based on gain-of-function perturbations in b. scDORI more accurately predicted regulatory directionality than SCENIC+, particularly for repressed targets. e, Percentage of Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) opened after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b, determined by ATAC-seq. Significance determined by one-sided hypergeometric test (BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Only the pioneer TF ASCL1 induced a strong and significant increase in chromatin accessibility across neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like Topic regions. f, Expression of top neuronal-like state regulators in GB states (left) and TME neurons (right) in our patient atlas. Dot colour and size indicate average expression and percentage of TF-expressing cells. MYT1L is the only TF exclusively expressed in neuronal-like GB cells at levels comparable to TME neurons. g, Genomic distribution of MYT1L-bound regions (n = 20,620) in S24 PDGCs determined by CUT&RUN after 8 days of MYT1L OE (n = 3) (top). Intensity of CUT&RUN peaks within ± 1 kb from peak summit in OE and control conditions (bottom). h, Differentially accessible regions (DARs) after MYT1L OE compared to control PDGCs in neurospheroid monoculture or co-culture with primary cortical cells (n = 3 each). Shown are the proportion of opening and closing regions, bound or not bound by MYT1L, and their genomic annotation. MYT1L predominantly closes chromatin by binding enhancer and promoter regions. i, Representative genome browser examples of MYT1L-bound TRs closed after MYT1L OE, as in b,g. j, Precision of MYT1L downstream target prediction, assessed at the level of target TFs and all target genes. Predicted MYT1L targets were derived from an average scDORI eGRN across neuronal-like Topics and compared against those of a SCENIC+ eGRN trained on neuronal-like cells. Blue boxes indicate the proportion of predicted targets directly bound by MYT1L (CUT&RUN as in g). Colours denote directional concordance with ATAC-seq and RNA-seq changes after MYT1L OE as in b. scDORI outperformed SCENIC+ in MYT1L regulon prediction, particularly at the TF level. Illustration in b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Chromatin and transcriptional changes induced by primary cortical co-culture on S24 PDGCs compared to neurospheroid monoculture (n = 3 each). Enriched Topic programs in differentially accessible genes (DAGs; nearest gene to differentially accessible peak, FDR < 0.05) and DEGs (fold change>1.5, FDR < 0.05) as determined by GSEA, and the percentage of opening and closing Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) are shown. Dot colour and size denote GSEA normalized enrichment score (NES) and significance, respectively. Asterisks indicate significant changes in Topic peaks (one-sided hypergeometric test, BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Co-culture broadly opens chromatin across multiple Topic regions, consistent with a plasticity-promoting environment. b, MYT1L levels after Dox-based manipulation in S24 PDGCs co-cultured with primary cortical cells, in therapy-naive and therapy-exposed contexts. (Left) Normalized MYT1L counts from bulk RNA-seq during MYT1L induction (day 6, on) and after withdrawal (day 6 post-dox removal, off), compared to matched controls. (Right) MYT1L levels quantified by qPCR in PDGCs pre-exposed to ionizing radiation or temozolomide (TMZ), with and without MYT1L induction (day 6), compared to untreated controls. n = 3 biological replicates per condition, except for Dox control (n = 2). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average state association score of differentially closed and opened genes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs with and without prior therapy exposure (ionizing radiation or temozolomide), as in b. Therapy-induced effects are shown below. Colour indicates z-scored state score. MYT1L represses non-neuronal-like gene signatures even under therapeutic pressure. d, Overlap of DAGs induced by MYT1L OE under therapeutic pressure with DAGs from MYT1L OE alone or treatment alone, all identified relative to untreated, unmanipulated controls as in b. Stacked bars show the proportion of closing (left) and opening (right) DAGs attributable to MYT1L OE alone, treatment alone, both, or neither. Most MYT1L-induced chromatin changes are preserved under both treatments, indicating that the plasticity-restricting function of MYT1L is largely retained under therapeutic pressure. e, Chromatin changes in Topic-associated regions and genes after MYT1L OE in therapy-exposed PDGCs in b, computed as in a with respect to untreated, unmanipulated controls. MYT1L-driven effects (Fig. 5f) are conserved under therapeutic pressure, albeit modestly attenuated. f, Representative western blots of MYT1L protein levels in S24 (n = 6 independent experiments, P = 1.8 × 10−6 OE vs control) and P3XX PDGCs (n = 5 independent experiments, P = 0.035 OE vs control), 7 days after MYT1L OE compared to controls, with fold-change quantifications. Uncropped Western blots are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. (Bottom) MYT1L expression by qPCR 3 weeks after MYT1L knockout (KO) in BG5 PDGCs compared to controls (n = 3 independent experiments, P = 0.072 KO vs control). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; two-sided t-test. g, Enriched Topic signatures in DEGs of MYT1L OE (S24, P3XX) or KO (BG5) compared to controls (n = 3 each), 3 weeks post-transduction, as determined by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. Neuronal-like identity is enriched after OE and depleted after KO. h, Selected pathways enriched after indicated MYT1L manipulations by GSEA. Dot colour and size denote NES and significance, respectively. All significantly enriched pathways are reported in Supplementary Table 10. MYT1L gain-of-function upregulates neuronal and synapse-related pathways, whereas loss of function upregulates stem cell pathways. i, Morphological changes after MYT1L OE in S24 PDGCs in neural microenvironments. (Left) Representative images of PDGC morphology in co-culture with primary hippocampal neurons (day 7; representative of ROIs quantified at right) and in mouse cortex xenografts (two-photon live imaging, 21 days post-injection; 6 z-stacked regions per mouse, n = 3 MYT1L OE and n = 2 control mice). (Right) Quantification of primary branches and total neurite-like projections from in vitro co-culture experiments (n = 16 control vs n = 17 MYT1L OE ROIs with 7–10 quantified cells per ROI; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE significantly increases the number and complexity of neurite-like projections. Data shown as mean ± s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=100 µm. j, Tumour microtube (TM) interconnectivity in S24 PDGCs monocultures after MYT1L OE (n = 48 control vs. n = 37 MYT1L OE ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments) or knockdown (KD) (n = 47 control vs n = 44 MYT1L KD ROIs; n = 3 independent experiments). MYT1L OE reduced, and KD increased average TM length, yielding fewer and more connected morphologies, respectively. (Right) Total cell counts per ROI confirm comparable cell numbers across conditions. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test are shown. Scale bar=200 µm. k, Proliferation time-course of PDGCs after MYT1L OE (S24; n = 5 independent experiments x 10 wells each) or KO (BG5; n = 3 independent experiments x 30 wells each) determined by Alamar Blue assay, normalized to day 0. MYT1L OE and KO significantly reduce and increase proliferation, respectively. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values from two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test are shown. l, Representative fluorescent microscopy images of tdTomato-labelled S24 PDGC spheroids transduced with Dox-inducible constructs of full-length MYT1L (left), MYT1L DBD fused with a VP64 activator domain (centre), or MYT1L DBD fused with an EnR repressor domain (right). Images of uninduced and dox-induced spheroids were taken on day 7 after embedding and binarized based on intensity. Dashed lines delineate spheroid size at day 0. Total number of spheroids and corresponding growth quantifications are shown in Fig. 5h. Scale bar=1,000 µm. m, Fold change in proliferation of S24 PDGCs after 7 days of OE of the indicated MYT1L constructs in l, normalized to uninduced controls. Full-length MYT1L and DBD–EnR reduced proliferation, while DBD–VP64 enhanced it. n = 8 wells x 3 independent experiments; Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d.; P-values for two-sided t-test against uninduced controls are shown. Illustrations in b,e,i,j created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

#1360. Russell must do something wacky now after disappointing Bahrain GP qualifying

Never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he said he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9

Tomorrow’s race will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start on the front row together. It is a reasonable run down to turn one and there are overtaking opportunities through the first few corners at Sepang, with it being similar to the configuration in China, with plenty of lines and moves on offer.

Respect between two great champions 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/fbZ6aoKRyw

“Very difficult to understand. We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is the different to all the (other) tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”

Lewis Hamilton says this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

“The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Big, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

QUALIFYING CLASSIFICATIONCan't wait for Sunday! 🤩#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/qqi8hPDcKA

“It is fantastic. We have been trying many grand prix to get pole. Sometimes a bit closer than others but to finally get it, from where we started the season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and, for sure, I am going to try and win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”

Big disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he said he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

Excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

*Hadjar’s three-place grid penalty will drop him down to eighth place for the race tomorrow.

Neither of the Red Bulls can improve in the first sector but it is those behind them who need significant improvements. The two Ferraris are going along nicely at the start of their final flying laps. Hadjar is unable to improve despite a purple final sector. Verstappen then goes fastest in the final sector and improves his advantage at the top.

Hamilton meanwhile went fastest in the middle sector and goes second fastest overall. Piastri cannot improve but stays ahead of Russell.

Norris is the final man across the line but is only fast enough for P6. That means that Verstappen takes pole in Malaysia, which is the first time this season that Red Bull have taken pole position. Hamilton is second with Hadjar third, although the Frenchman has a five-place grid penalty.

MAX VERSTAPPEN TAKES POLE FOR THE BAHRAIN GRAND PRIX IN MALAYSIA!! 👊#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/NgtaCAZacL

The two Red Bulls, who are one and two at the moment, will be the first two drivers across the line on these final efforts.

The other nine drivers in Q3 are in the pits so young Antonelli has the track to himself as he sets his one and only flying lap of Q3. He is over four tenths down on Verstappen through the first sector and has plenty of work to do.

The championship leader sets a decent middle sector where he loses no more time to Verstappen. As it stands he would put himself third before the others do their final runs. He comes across the line in P3 but will have the likes of Hamilton, Piastri, Leclerc, Norris and Russell trying to surpass him.

Russell is the first across the line and sets a time of a 1:36.032. He does not last long at the top as he is immediately displaced by Hadjar, who is half a second quicker.

Hamilton then comes over the line in second, just ahead of his teammate Leclerc. Piastri puts himself between the two Ferraris.

What about Verstappen? The man who won here the last time we were in Malaysia continues his great form today and goes quickest by more than three tenths.

Antonelli now heads out and will have the track to himself really. This is going to be the championship leader’s only flying lap of Q3.

Russell is the first man to head out for his first flying lap in Q3. Antonelli has remained in the pits with just one new set of softs remaining. Verstappen, who right now feels like the favourite for pole, will be one of the last across the line in these first attempts of Q3.

The fight for pole position in Sepang begins now as the green light is on at the end of the pit lane to get Q3 going.

Antonelli, due to that lap time deletion in Q2, has just one new set of softs for Q3, which could prove costly in his attempts to try and take pole.

P12 the best qualifying result of the season for Alonso. It was only his second time in Q2 after Hungary (P16).

I should add, P14 was also Lance Stroll’s best qualifying result of the season. His first outing in Q2 this year.

11. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls)12. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)13. Carlos Sainz (Williams)14. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)

With grid penalties already on their way, neither Colapinto nor Lindblad set lap times in Q2.

Verstappen, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris, Hadjar and Russell all remain in the pits. A bit of a risk for Russell down in eighth but his time should be enough to get into Q3.

Lindblad, who will start tomorrow’s race at the back of the grid after penalties, gives his teammate Lawson a tow down the back straight and it works as Lawson just sneaks into the top ten.

Can Bortoleto get back ahead though of Lawson? Yes he can and he will take the final place in Q3. Lawson thought he might be through but the tow was not enough.

Lindblad, who's taking a grid penalty for Sunday's race, gave team mate Lawson a tow but it wasn't quite enough to send the Kiwi into Q3#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/IMlrqg4ENv

As the young Italian starts his flying lap, there is no-one else out on track so no traffic. He is a lot more cautious at turn six this time than last time, when he had his lap time deleted.

He has not set blistering first and second sector times but a purple final sector puts him into second and the Italian is safely into Q3.

Plenty of other drivers are now heading around the track for their final flying laps of Q2.

11. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)12. Carlos Sainz (Williams)13. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)14. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)15. Franco Colapinto (Alpine)16. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)

Mercedes have put a brand new set of softs onto Antonelli’s car as he heads out promptly, with no lap time to his name so far. Antonelli is still disputing the lap deletion over team radio but his team tell him the images show he exceeded track limits. This is now a lot of pressure on the championship leader; any mistake now and he will not make Q3. His teammate Russell is only in seventh.

Antonelli was fourth fastest but has had his lap time deleted for exceeding track limits at turn six. That is a big moment in Q2 and could prove problematic if he gets into Q3. Antonelli appeared to be confused when he was told about his lap deletion over team radio but the on-board view looked pretty clear-cut.

Piastri then comes across the line in third.

Here's the moment Kimi ran wide 👀#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/E0VdWdBt8x

The Dutchman looks in a great spot at the moment to take pole position today and his 1:35.696 is very quick. He is nearly four tenths quicker than Antonelli.

How about the Ferraris? Leclerc was quickest in the middle sector but is nearly three tenths down on Verstappen. Hamilton puts himself into third place. Russell is more than half a second down on Verstappen.

Verstappen has been shown a black and white flag for driving unnecessarily slowly. I doubt he will get a grid penalty for that but it will be a warning for the Dutchman.

Anyway, the drivers, other than Colapinto and Alonso, are on flying laps, with Verstappen currently fastest inthe first sector.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and the second part of qualifying is under way. Like the start of Q1, it is hardly a stampede to go out.

17. Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)18. Oliver Bearman (Haas)19. Esteban Ocon (Haas)20. Alex Albon (Williams)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

The Aston Martin of Stroll improves significantly from 20th and is set to make Q2, as is his teammate Alonso. A bit of a surprise to see the Aston Martins improve and make it into Q2.

Go Fernando! 🤩 Go Lance! 🤩First double Q2 appearance this season 🙌#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/xjiWYv6ycr

That has seen the Audi of Hulkenberg drop into the drop zone and the German is out. For contrast, his teammate improves to go into eighth place! Hulkenberg had a big lock up into turn 14, which proved very costly.

As it stands, eight of the top nine are remaining in the garage. Russell is in ninth and has not gone out but Gasly above him in eighth has. You would imagine Russell is perfectly safe.

17. Esteban Ocon (Haas)18. Alex Albon (Williams)19. Oliver Bearman (Haas)20. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)21. Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac)

Ocon, in 17th, is quite far off Hulkenberg in 16th and needs more than four tenths to usurp him.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he says Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he said. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

He added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”

The two Ferraris are on medium tyres but Leclerc still puts himself into second place. He is then displaced by Hamilton, who slots in behind Verstappen. Good times from the Ferraris on the mediums.

What about the McLarens? Norris goes sixth fastest but is more than six tenths down on Verstappen. Then comes Piastri, who goes fourth fastest, just under four tenths off Verstappen.

Arguably the three favourites for pole; Antonelli, Russell and Verstappen, are all on flying laps.

The first sector goes the way of Verstappen, who is purple, and then the Dutchman goes purple in the middle sector.

Antonelli is two tenths faster than his teammate Russell but Verstappen is over half a second quicker than the Mercedes. Hadjar is then second fastest to show the pace in the Red Bull this weekend.

Most of the teams waited and waited to come out and then suddenly lots of drivers are sent out, resulting in a queue in the pits! With the high track temperatures and high degradation, the drivers are crawling around on their out laps to preserve these soft tyres.

Bumper to bumper in the pit lane! #F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/ff8JO9kB1g

The two Haas drivers have a free track to themselves whilst everyone else bides their time. In theory, as the hour of qualifying goes on, the track temperature should decrease and the more rubber that is laid down the faster the track should get.

Finally, just before the two Haas drivers finish their first flying laps, the rest of the grid is starting to emerge, led by the Mercedes duo.

The green light is showing at the end of the pit lane and Q1 is officially under way. The two Haas drivers are the first to head out. Other than that, it is a quiet start to Q1.

The top four teams; Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren, all have a genuine chance of taking pole in Sepang today. I think the true favourites though have to be the Mercedes duo and Max Verstappen but with how close it between all four of the teams you cannot rule anything out.

It is 33 degrees celsius air temperature, with the track temperature up at 58 degrees.

Not long to wait now until qualifying begins. It is hot, humid and dry in Sepang right now. As we know in Malaysia, the weather can change quickly and thunderstorms can roll in quite quickly but it looks like today’s qualifying will be a dry one. This will be one of if not the hottest qualifying sessions of the season, so much so that we are seeing umbrellas going up to get some shade from the sun rather than sheltering from any rain.

This will be important to consider after qualifying finishes as there will be some shuffling around:

Isack Hadjar (Red Bull): five-place grid penalty- new internal combustion engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): ten-place grid penalty- new engineFranco Colapinto (Alpine): five-place grid penalty- causing a collision in BakuArvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls): back of the grid- complete power unit change

Hadjar has looked good since returning from his wrist injury so could be fighting it out near the front of the grid, although his five-place penalty will drop him down. We know Lindblad will be at the back and is very likely to be joined there by Colapinto, who is not going to be qualifying high up in the top ten in his Alpine.

Haas have announced that Frenchman Esteban Ocon will leave at the end of this season. Ocon now faces an uncertain future, with it difficult to see a spot for him on the F1 grid next season. There are suggestions that the 30-year-old’s replacement will be Brazilian Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, although nothing has been confirmed on that front. 21-year-old Camara currently leads the Formula 2 championship.

TGR Haas F1 Team and Esteban Ocon will part ways at the conclusion of the 2026 season. With plenty of racing ahead, our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year.#HaasF1 #F1 pic.twitter.com/4iQAuqnSyA

Aston Martin have now confirmed their driver line-up for next season, retaining both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll. There had been reports that Alonso had been contemplating retirement but the 45-year-old will continue into another season.

Aston Martin Aramco confirms Lance and Fernando will continue as the team's drivers in 2027. Read more: ​https://t.co/ePyjJdyAIB pic.twitter.com/VogFUEbNxy

Other than the second seat alongside Ollie Bearman at Haas, the only other team to keep an eye on is Racing Bulls, with no definite confirmation on their exact driver line-up for next season.

Ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to issue a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

“Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti said. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

“The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. Here they are and who they were racing for:

Max Verstappen (Red Bull) Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes) Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes) Esteban Ocon (Force India)Nico Hulkenberg (Renault)Sergio Perez (Force India)Fernando Alonso (McLaren)Lance Stroll (Williams)Carlos Sainz (Toro Rosso)Pierre Gasly (Toro Rosso)

With Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

Last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a new floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

This race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

#1359. Europa League: How many points Milan and Juventus need to qualify

Juventus and Milan are heading in opposite directions in the Europa League, and a new projection shows exactly how many points each will need to reach the knockout stage.

According to Corriere dello Sport, data platform Football Meets Data has calculated the likely qualification marks with four games of the league phase left.

Ten points should be enough to finish in the top 24 and reach the playoffs, with a 95% chance of qualifying. Nine points drops that to just 52.8%.

Reaching the last 16 directly will be harder. A top-eight finish with 15 points comes with only a 50.9% chance. That rises to 89.4% with 16 points and 99.6% with 17. Goal difference could also decide places for teams level on points.

Luciano Spalletti’s Juventus are already on 10 points and unbeaten after Thursday’s 2-1 win at AZ Alkmaar. Teun Koopmeiners scored against his former club, and Randal Kolo Muani added a second. Two more wins would put them on the verge of the last 16.

Milan face a much tougher task. Rúben Amorim’s side lost 2-0 at home to Ferencváros, with Lenny Joseph scoring both goals. They have just three points from four games and have dropped to 28th, outside the playoff places. They probably need at least seven points from their last four matches.

I pray Milan to be kicked out early they have nothing to show

#1357. CELTIC 3 BESIKTAS 2: Duran and Osmand make the difference from the bench as O'Neill's men roar back to claim precious victory

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:33 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:56 EDT, 5 November 2026

By the time the Celtic players had reacquainted themselves with the concept of a lap of honour on a European night, those who had come to decry the club’s hierarchy had shuffled off into the night.

This somewhat unexpected outcome saved Martin O’Neill from the ignominy of being the first manager in the history of the Parkhead club to suffer five straight losses in European competition.

It should also lower the temperature in the ongoing feud between the directors and the fanbase for a few days at least.

After a diabolical start to their Europa League campaign, O’Neill’s men are belatedly up and running. The task of accruing sufficient points to reach the knock-out round again is still enormous although it is not yet beyond them. There’s life in this yet.

Of the four sides who Celtic were drawn to play in Glasgow in this phase, Besiktas looked the most imposing. In taking their scalp, O’Neill’s side will have received a much-needed infusion of self-belief. An inexorable slide towards a full-blown crisis has been avoided, for now.

This was quite the night. A drab and goalless first half was no indication of what was to come.

Camilo Duran squeezes home the winner in the 87th minute for Celtic

Substitutes Callum Osmand (left) and Camilo Duran turned the tide for Celtic

O’Neill’s men fell behind through a penalty but, to their enormous credit, they did not wilt.

So much of the credit for a famous triumph belonged to two players who, oddly, didn’t start the match.

Callum Osmand levelled with his first touch and was scintillating in everything he did from that point on.

Camilo Duran, another who’d started the night clad in a tracksuit, edged O’Neill’s side in front following a majestic ball from Osmand.

When Besiktas levelled with five minutes remaining, many of the home supporters would probably have settled for a draw. Not a bit of it. Duran’s second of the night, two minutes later, secured a magnificent victory, one which might just prove to be a turning point.

For those arriving in the stadium and checking their phones, O’Neill’s team selection required a second take. After playing just 31 minutes across three substitute appearances, Jordan Lotomba was handed his first start at right back ahead of Colby Donovan.

James Forrest and Sebastian Tounekti were deployed on the flanks with Kasper Hogh selected in place of Duran at centre-forward. So much for a must-win game.

There was familiarity in the Besiktas side in the shape of former Rangers winger Vaclav Cerny and Oh Hyeon-gyu, formerly a striker in this parish.

Although the Turks controlled the first half, Celtic did fashion the first real opening. Mika Baur fed Tounekti who squared the ball to Benjamin Nygren. The Swede ought to have done much better than fire wildly over.

Celtic’s attempt to press high was admirable. All too often, though, the men in black just played through it.

Forrest did well to move the ball on and invited Lotomba to attack it. He was easily brushed aside.

Duran celebrates making it 2-1 in a thrilling second half at Parkhead

It became a recurring theme. Not only were Besiktas technically superior to Celtic in the opening half, collectively, they were physically stronger. If there was a 50/50 to be won, invariably, they won it.

The upshot was that O’Neill’s men made little headway when they got into promising positions.

It said much that the biggest roar of the first half from the home supporters came when Liam Scales took ball then man – that man being Cerny.

You had to wonder what instructions Sam Johnstone had been given. His tactic of launching the ball long to Hogh was, to say the least, optimistic. With next to nothing coming from the flanks, the Dane was again starved of service.

The encouraging thing for O’Neill at the break was the fact that Besiktas’ possession hadn’t translated into too many chances. Cerny fired over. Leandro Trossard forced Johnstone into a good stop, although the offside flag had been raised.

Tounekti contributed another uninspiring display. Time and again, he gathered the ball on the flank. If there was an easy option to take, he took it.

The Tunisian had a chance to play Forrest in after creeping infield. Remarkably, he managed to stumble on the ball and Besiktas sprang another attack.

Although Celtic were level at the break, they’d been feckless. A chance to fashion something from a free-kick saw Tounekti pick out Nygren. The Swede completely lost his footing and the chance was gone.

Callum McGregor was the most relieved man in the ground in the opening seconds of the second period. He turned into trouble on the edge of his own box in the shape of Junior Olaitan and watched as Trossard’s curler flew just over.

Another old head in Forrest came close at the other end, his slalom from right to centre ending with a low shot which the keeper fielded.

Lotomba’s display throughout was poor, entirely in keeping with a player with so little football under his belt.

Osmand made an instant impact in rifling home for 1-1 from the edge of the box

It was no surprise that the error which led to Besiktas’ opener came from him. Johnstone created the initial problem by needlessly smashing a clearance off the frame of Trossard. It broke kindly to Ernest Poku. With no need to panic, Lotomba did exactly that. His scything of his opponent was a clear penalty.

Johnstone stood up to block Olaitan’s initial effort but couldn’t recover in time. The Besiktas man smashed home the rebound once the ball had fallen from the night sky. It was scarcely ill-deserved at that point.

O’Neill threw on Duran, Osmand and Donovan. The changes yielded an immediate return.

Advanced on the left of the box, McGregor showed composure to square the ball to Osmand. Any fears of ring-rust from the substitute were misplaced. A crisp right-foot shot flew into the bottom corner to level.

Credit where it’s due. Having hardly worried the Turks up to that stage, Celtic found something. Scales had his head in his hands after being denied a headed goal from a corner by a smart save by Alexander Nobel in the Besiktas goal.

With Osmand’s work rate giving the home fans something to get behind, Celtic improved. Another surge by the forward brought Hogh into the game. Duran’s pace took him into a dangerous position but the Dane couldn’t find him.

Osmand then fed the advanced Nygren. Again, the normally dependable Swede didn’t have his shooting boots on.

The former Fulham player seemed to be everywhere. It was his brilliantly measured pass which cut the Turkish defence wide open as Celtic turned the game on its head with 78 minutes remaining.

Perfectly weighted and angled, it still asked a lot of Duran. The Colombian did brilliantly, gathering and rounding the keeper in the blink of an eye then rolling the ball into an empty net.

As Celtic Park rejoiced, substitute Haissem Hassan fizzed one into the keeper’s arms.

How O’Neill’s men would come to rue that moment. There didn’t appear to be much on when substitute Orkun Kokcu took aim 25 yards out and thundered the ball low past Johnstone.

A slow burner of a game had certainly sprang into life. And we weren’t done yet.

Celtic dusted themselves down and came again. Donovan motored across the field and found Tierney. The full-back’s strike didn’t have the power to trouble the keeper but fell kindly for Duran. At the second attempt, he bundled the ball home.

Aston Villa are reportedly preparing an offer to sign River Plate goalkeeper Santiago Beltran ahead of the January transfer window, as Unai Emery looks to strengthen his squad.

According to a report from El Transigente, the Premier League club is considering a bid worth $10–15 million for the 22-year-old Argentine goalkeeper. Villa are keen to secure his services, although River Plate have yet to reveal whether they would be willing to negotiate his departure.

Beltran has established himself as an exciting young prospect at River Plate since earning promotion to the senior squad in early 2025. He was initially seen as a potential successor to experienced goalkeeper Franco Armani and impressed with his performances.

The Argentine has made 45 appearances for the South American giants, conceding 36 goals and keeping 19 clean sheets. Although some inconsistent performances have attracted criticism, his potential has not gone unnoticed, with several European clubs monitoring his progress.

Villa could provide him with an excellent opportunity to continue his development in European football.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Villa have already made changes to their goalkeeping department following Emiliano Martinez’s departure during the summer. They subsequently brought in Japanese international Zion Suzuki, who is expected to remain their first-choice goalkeeper.

However, Emery is seemingly interested in adding another promising option between the posts. Beltran could offer valuable competition for Suzuki while providing the Birmingham outfit with a long-term investment.

River Plate, however, could make negotiations difficult for the Premier League side. The Argentine club are reportedly working on a contract extension that could increase the goalkeeper’s release clause to $100 million.

Such a development would significantly strengthen River Plate’s negotiating position and make a January transfer considerably more complicated.

It remains to be seen whether Aston Villa will follow through with their proposed offer and whether River Plate will entertain negotiations for their highly rated goalkeeper.

#1355. Como president Suwarso: ‘We want to recruit like Brentford and Brighton and become like Barcelona’

Como president Mirwan Suwarso says the club want to play like Barcelona while recruiting like Brighton and Brentford, as their rise continues on two fronts.

Suwarso was speaking to TNT Sports commentator Adam Summerton in an exclusive interview. It came days after Como’s record-breaking 9-1 win over Lens, the biggest win by an Italian side in Champions League history.

“If you’re talking about recruitment, obviously Brighton and Brentford have become the model everybody looks at,” Suwarso said. “But we start from the DNA. What is our football? How do we want to play? So that it remains to be as such, even long after many changes in coaching positions.

“In terms of football DNA, we want to become like Barcelona. We want to have that focus on wanting to have the ball, high pressing, possession, which is attractive football. At the same time, we’re trying to find undervalued players we can fit into the unit using the same models as Brighton or Brentford have done.”

The Hartono brothers bought Como in Serie D seven years ago. Cesc Fabregas arrived as a player in 2022 and has since taken them into the Champions League as coach.

Fabregas’ side are fourth in Serie A on 23 points. They can move above Inter, the reigning champions, with a win at San Siro on Sunday, which kicks off at 18:00 CET [17:00 GMT].

Suwarso believes Serie A can close the gap to the Premier League. “Time. I think we need time,” he said. “I do believe every product, just like every economy, is cyclical. The Premier League may be at the top right now, but Serie A was as well. Nothing stays at the top forever, and even as we speak, the comparison of Serie A from last year to this year is almost night and day.

“The teams are becoming more attacking. So many young players, so many exciting, offensive players, without anyone probably doing it on purpose.”

He also revealed Como are now selling their expertise to other clubs. “The ideas that work, we are now starting to export them to offer them as services or as products to other clubs, because the revenue from one club is limited,” he explained. “Right now we’re working with 27 clubs. The revenue becomes scalable.”

Suwarso also hit back at critics of the project, insisting Italian football is more collaborative than it looks. “I think in Italy, what makes it to the media is not a true reflection of the reality,” he said. “The reality is actually very collaborative, and we are all trying to grow because we all have the same goal.”

Liverpool are reportedly demanding at least €70 million to sell Alexis Mac Allister, with Real Madrid interested in securing the Argentine midfielder ahead of the January transfer window.

According to a report from Spain, the Spanish giants have been informed of Liverpool’s financial demands, with the Premier League club unwilling to consider offers below their valuation of the 27-year-old.

Real Madrid are keen to strengthen their midfield options, and Mac Allister has emerged as one of Jose Mourinho’s preferred targets. The Argentine international could add technical quality, creativity and tactical versatility to the Spanish side’s midfield.

Liverpool are reportedly prepared to use the money generated from his potential departure to fund their own midfield rebuild. Despite his estimated transfer value being around €61.9 million, the Reds are holding out for a considerably higher figure.

The Merseyside outfit could therefore make negotiations difficult for Real Madrid, who will need to commit substantial funds to bring the World Cup winner to the Santiago Bernabeu.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Meanwhile, Mac Allister’s contractual situation could complicate matters further. His current agreement with Liverpool runs until June 2028, but the club have yet to offer him an extension.

The midfielder has previously expressed disappointment over the lack of progress regarding a new contract, particularly after seeing teammates Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai receive improved terms.

Real Madrid could view the situation as an opportunity to secure an important addition to their squad. The Spanish giants are looking for a long-term midfield solution following the departures of Luka Modric and Toni Kroos.

Mac Allister’s ability to dictate proceedings, retain possession and contribute defensively makes him an attractive option. Talks between the clubs could begin in December, with Real Madrid reportedly considering a formal €70 million proposal in early January.

However, Liverpool’s firm stance means the Spanish outfit will have to meet their financial demands to stand a realistic chance of completing the deal.
