Aligned with the synergistic effect of food odours and visual motion on arousal, we found that individual D. erecta males on ACV displayed more vigorous courtship when part of a larger group (five pairs of conspecifics) than when presented with just a single female in isolation—an effect not observed in D. melanogaster (Fig. 5h). Courtship towards a conspecific female was similarly enhanced by the presence of a same-sized group of Drosophila simulans, underscoring that these courtship-promoting cues are not species-specific (Fig. 5i). Moreover, male courtship in D. erecta was elevated by simply projecting two continuously rotating dots onto the assay chamber floor, highlighting that visual motion is sufficient to promote arousal (Fig. 5j and Supplementary Video 10).

Male courtship in D. erecta thus appears to be influenced by both the chemosensory environment of a food patch and the dynamic motion of the social group on it. To explore the composite effects of food odour and visual motion, we recorded the group dynamics of five pairs of D. erecta males and females on agar or ACV, approximated each fly’s centroid position as a high-contrast ellipse and then played back these visual motion cues to a ‘test’ D. erecta male and female pair (Fig. 5k and Supplementary Video 11). We observed that courtship in D. erecta males was enhanced by playback of the visual scene recorded from flies interacting on ACV (Fig. 5l). Courtship of the test pair on ACV was comparable when presented with either the visual scene recorded on agar or the scene recorded on ACV but slowed to match the velocity of flies on agar. D. erecta males therefore appear to be sensitive to the speed of visual targets, rather than their distinct dynamics. Notably, males on ACV, presented with the visual motion cues recorded on ACV, displayed the highest level of courtship, supporting the synergistic effects of the chemosensory and visual environment. Neither the presence of ACV nor playback of the social scenes recorded on ACV further increased the vigorous courtship displayed by D. melanogaster (Fig. 5m). Together, our data indicate that the chemosensory environment of a food patch promotes and perpetuates a male’s sexual arousal in D. erecta by driving males to sample and pursue visual targets, which in turn reshapes the visual social scene to further reinforce mating behaviours (Fig. 5n).

In Drosophila, courtship unfolds as a tightly coupled feedback loop between prospective mates, continuously shaped by the reciprocal exchange of sensory signals between male and female. Here we examined how this feedback loop is influenced by the ecological and social context of mating sites, showing that in D. erecta, both the olfactory volatiles emanating from a food patch and the collective dynamics of flies congregating there coordinately control courtship. We find that food odour regulates male courtship in D. erecta through two distinct mechanisms: first, by gating a male’s arousal to promote pursuit of potential mates; and second, by further enhancing his arousal through the increased visual motion of other individuals on the food patch, creating a feedback loop that elevates courtship in environments where reproductive opportunities are likely to be most abundant. D. erecta has thus evolved a striking dependence on environmental cues as an integral part of its reproductive strategy.

D. erecta’s distinct sensitivity to its environment may represent an adaptation well aligned with its specialization on Pandanus fruit, a seasonally restricted host that is only transiently available for reproduction. Breeding populations of D. erecta surge during the two-to-four-month period when Pandanus fruit is present and then sharply decline as the availability of fruit wanes21,22. During seasons when Pandanus is scarce, D. erecta can opportunistically subsist on other fruits, but in greatly diminished numbers, pointing to the inherent cost of specialization on ephemeral resources21,22. Although it remains unclear whether D. erecta’s reliance on food odours for mating is a direct adaptation to the seasonality of its host, such strict dependence underscores how Pandanus serves as a key ecological hub supporting the reproductive cycle of this species.

Variable access to mating sites, however, is not limited to D. erecta, as many drosophilids use fleeting host substrates to reproduce15,17,24. The chemosensory environment of mating sites may therefore modulate sexual arousal more generally. Consistent with this, the ability of ACV to promote courtship appears to be maintained in a latent form across Drosophila species, emerging only when males are presented with a relatively impoverished two-dimensional visual target (Extended Data Fig. 5) or in darkness7. Likewise, ACV has been shown to alter the salience of visual objects during flight in D. melanogaster40, indicating that the arousing effect of food volatiles is broadly conserved, with its behavioural expression quantitatively tuned by species-specific sensory thresholds. The modulation of reproductive behaviours by chemosensory cues not directly related to sexual signalling thus seems an evolutionarily malleable trait, shaped by the ecology and social landscape in which species evolve. Indeed, although ACV, a chemical mimic of fermenting substrates, enhances the sexual arousal of species that mate on decaying fruit, it inhibits courtship in the flower breeder D. elegans. Sexual arousal can therefore be enhanced or suppressed by environmental contexts, underscoring the bidirectional influence of the chemical environment on reproductive behaviour.

In D. erecta, the sensory threshold for arousal appears to be particularly high, rendering sustained courtship strictly dependent on continuous olfactory input. Indeed, transient activation of P1 neurons is insufficient to drive the persistent pursuit that other Drosophila species display37,38, indicating that olfactory input acts downstream of P1 neurons or on other circuit elements to perpetuate a male’s arousal. Consistent with this idea, ACV not only sustains P1-mediated arousal but can independently promote courtship pursuit. Although the precise neural locus of ACV’s action remains to be elucidated, the comparable activation of Dsx+ neurons in D. erecta, D. melanogaster and D. yakuba suggests that species-specific gating of courtship reflects quantitative reweighting of conserved olfactory inputs rather than recruitment of novel pathways. For example, D. melanogaster can become highly aroused through visual input alone, consistent with evidence that subsets of P1 neurons receive direct LC10a input34. P1 neuron activity in turn modulates the gain of LC10a responses38, forming a recurrent circuit poised to perpetuate visually guided courtship pursuit. One intriguing possibility is that ACV-responsive olfactory pathways gate this feedback loop in D. erecta, such that both vision and food volatiles are required for males to sustain their sexual arousal.

Such subtle variation in conserved elements of courtship circuits underscores how these pathways can diversify while maintaining their core function, enabling different species to rapidly adapt to their distinct ecological needs41. This flexibility may be facilitated by their modular architecture. Pheromone responses in P1 neurons, for example, are unaffected by ACV (Fig. 4h), and responses of Dsx+ neurons in the LPC to pheromones and ACV are spatially distinct (Extended Data Fig. 8), indicating that olfactory and pheromonal pathways remain at least partly segregated. Such an organization may preserve the ability of males to discriminate between conspecific and heterospecific females even when highly aroused on a food patch (Extended Data Fig. 9a). The modularity of courtship circuits36,42,43 thus favours the independent diversification of distinct circuit elements, allowing D. erecta to evolve behavioural sensitivity to environmental cues and exploit fleeting reproductive opportunities such as those provided by its host fruit.

Beyond the direct modulation of circuits perpetuating sexual arousal, ACV also serves to structure the social landscape at multiple levels. First, ACV triggers D. erecta flies to rapidly track to the odour source. Flies in our experiments were fed and sated, suggesting their aggregation on a food patch is driven by reproductive rather than metabolic needs. Second, once on the food patch, ACV promotes males to sample visual targets, presumably in search of sexually receptive females, transforming the visual scene through their collective motion during this form of ‘social foraging’. Finally, because D. erecta males are highly sensitive to visual motion, their courtship is further enhanced by the presence of moving visual targets. This in turn orchestrates the behaviour of nearby individuals such that their bouts of pursuit become synchronized, an effect most apparent on agar, where periods of immobility are punctuated by intermittent bursts of activity across the group.

Aggregating in larger groups increases a male’s access to potential mating partners but at the same time promotes competition, which is thought to be fierce on a crowded food patch44,45. Reproductive success in these competitive environments requires that males fend off their rivals and isolate a female for long enough to initiate copulation46. As a consequence, a male’s sensitivity to visual motion may confer an advantage in gaining access to potential mating opportunities by triggering him to chase after any visual object that may be a receptive female or courting pair. Indeed, on a food patch, males become attracted to all visual objects and indiscriminately approach a male, a female or a bead (Extended Data Fig. 2d). The drive to compete therefore likely structures the collective activity observed in groups of D. erecta.

Although Drosophila is not typically thought to engage in collective social behaviours, the dynamics of D. erecta on a food patch may follow the same principles that structure schooling fish13, swarming locusts12 or murmurations of starlings14,47. In these systems, simple local interaction rules—such as attraction and repulsion among neighbours—align the behaviour of many individuals into concerted actions12,48,49. Likewise, in D. erecta aggregates, the behaviour of neighbouring flies serves as an environmental reference that modulates courtship behaviour: not through direct signalling between prospective sexual partners, but through generic visual motion cues that indicate the broader environmental context. However, in contrast to canonical examples of collective behaviours—where information is thought to be cooperatively shared to optimize the fitness of all individuals in the group—D. erecta’s sensitivity to group dynamics probably evolved to enhance individual reproductive fitness to succeed in a competitive environment. Our results thus indicate that collective behaviours can emerge from diverse selective pressures, giving rise to coordinated actions even in species not generally considered ‘social’.

Flies were housed at 25 °C and 50–65% relative humidity on a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle, except for animals used in optogenetics experiments, which were reared in darkness. Stocks used for behavioural experiments were reared on standard molasses food, 2P imaging lines were reared on Würzburg food for at least five generations to increase animal robustness, and flies expressing optogenetic actuators were kept on sugar-yeast food to prevent intake of the cofactor retinal. Fly stocks used were as follows: D. melanogaster stocks 71G01-Gal4 (39599) and UAS-GCaMP6s (42746) were obtained from Bloomington Stock Center. Canton-S (G. Maimon, Rockefeller University), CO4n and RG11n (J. Pool, University of Wisconsin-Madison), UAS-CsChrimson (V. Jayaraman, Janelia Research Campus) and VT029314 (LC10a)-LexA, LexAop-GCaMP6s (I. Ribeiro and B. Dickson, Janelia Research Campus) were generously shared by the indicated colleagues. Wild-type D. erecta (14021-0224.01), w− D. erecta (14021-0224.07) and D. yakuba (14021-0261.00) were obtained from the Cornell Stock Center. Ruta lab D. simulans, D. orena (D. Stern, Janelia Research Campus), D. erecta 71G01-Gal4, UAS-GCaMP6s, UAS-CsChrimson, ppk23-mutant and D. erecta as well as D. yakuba Dsx-Gal4 (Y. Ding, University of Pennsylvania) were previously generated36 or shared by the indicated colleagues. D. erecta VT029314 (LC10a)-Gal4, Fru-Gal4, Orco-Gal4 (for labelling, see Extended Data Fig. 10), ∆Orco and ∆Ir8a were generated in this study. The 71G01-Gal4 driver labels a subset of approximately 1052 out of 78 highly interconnected P1 neurons described in D. melanogaster34 and a similar number of neurons in D. erecta36.

Vector backbone pRC12B36 with ie1.mCherry minigene reporter was used to clone the synthesized VT029314 enhancer fragment gBlock (IDT) upstream of Gal4 by means of Gibson assembly (NEB). The construct was co-injected with hyTsps mRNA into embryos for transposase-mediated genome integration. Chemosensory coreceptor knockouts were generated by targeted excision of the first three exons (Orco) or the entire coding region (Ir8a) using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair inserting a fluorescent marker gene cassette encoding mCherry under the viral ie1 promoter (Orco) or RFP under control of D. melanogaster 3xP3 (Ir8a). The Orco-Gal4 line in D. erecta was generated by cloning 5,496 bp upstream of the Orco translation start site upstream of the Gal4 sequence into the pCaSpeR backbone and a gateway cassette (pCaSpeR-DEST3 (DGRC, 1029; Research Resource Identifier: DGRC_1029)). The Fru-Gal4 line was generated by first establishing an attP landing site in the D. erecta fruitless locus and subsequently inserting a splice acceptor-Gal4 element. The landing site was created using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated cleavage to the intron 5′ of the exon containing the ATG start codon (as previously described)53 with homology-directed repair inserting the attP sequence. The resulting validated fruattP line was used as a target for site-specific integration of a splice acceptor-Gal4 element, which contained an ie1.mCherry transformation marker.

All transgenic lines in D. erecta were made in a wild-type genetic background except the Orco-Gal4 line, which was constructed in a w− background. For experiments, all constructs were crossed into a wild-type (w+) background to exclude potential behavioural effects of the w− mutation.

Adult brains were dissected in Schneider’s media (Sigma) and immediately transferred to cold 1% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) for overnight fixation at 4 °C. Samples were then washed three times in PAT3 buffer (0.5% bovine serum albumin, 0.5% Triton, phosphate-buffered saline pH 7.4). Brains were blocked in 3% Normal Goat Serum for 90 min at room temperature and incubated in primary antibodies (1:1,000 chicken anti-GFP (Abcam, ab13970), 1:50 mouse anti-brp (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank nc82)) for 3 h at room temperature followed by an overnight incubation step at 4 °C. Brains were then washed three times in PAT3 buffer and once in phosphate-buffered saline. Brains were mounted in Vectashield (Vector Laboratories). Images were captured on a Zeiss LSM 880 using a Plan-Apochromat ×20 (0.8 numerical aperture) objective.

All free-walking behavioural assays were conducted at 25 °C and 50–65% relative humidity between 0 and 3 h after lights on. Virgin males and females were collected after eclosion and group-housed separated by sex for 4–7 days before the assay. Flies were aspirated without anaesthesia, females first followed by males. All free-behaviour videos were recorded with FlyCapture 2 (v.2.13.3.61) at 30 or 42 frames per second (fps) in back light from a white light pad (Logan Electric) using a Point Grey FLIR Grasshopper camera (GS3-U3-32S4M-C 3MP) fitted with a HF12.5SA-1 lens (Fujinon). Central food patches of varying sizes (see below) were formed either from agar (2% w/v) perfumed with ACV (20% v/v), agar (2% w/v) with P. candelabrum fruit pulp (20%) or a 2% agar-only control.

Assays were performed in 190-mm-diameter, 3-mm-high circular slope-walled Delrin chambers with a central food patch of 21.5 mm diameter. Five females were transferred to the chamber by mouth aspiration followed by five males. Once the males were loaded, the assay commenced, and groups were recorded for 40 min. Single-individual assays lasted 20 min. The centroid position of each fly was tracked in every frame, and identity swaps were manually corrected using the Caltech FlyTracker (v.1.0.5)54. The positional data were then used to infer individual trajectories, relative distributions and the distance of flies to the central food patch in MATLAB (v.2023b, MathWorks). A clustering fly was defined as within 3 fly lengths of at least one other fly, whereas a solitary individual was defined as being at a distance of at least 3 fly lengths from all other flies in the arena. The timing and position of copulations were manually scored.

Grid assays were conducted in modified large 190-mm-diameter arenas with a large 145-mm-diameter central food patch. A grid forming a lattice of 13 black, fly-sized (3 mm diameter) hemispherical plastic beads (Etsy) arranged in a regular square array was placed on the patch. The grid consisted of five equidistant beads along the horizontal midline with a distance of 30 mm along the edge, three equidistant beads 30 mm above and below and one more bead 30 mm above and below the three beads, all aligned along the midline. Assays with either five males or a single solitary male were recorded for 20 min. For ‘social foraging’ assays, one randomly chosen bead of the grid was exchanged with an immobilized decapitated female. Recording commenced after aspiration of all males. The centroid position and speed of each fly was tracked in every frame using AnimalTA (v.3.2.2)55. If necessary, identity swaps were corrected manually in the software. Exact bead positions were extracted for each assay using the same software. Distances of males to beads or the immobilized female and visits to visual targets were calculated from the positional data and used to infer individual trajectories and relative distributions. Summary statistics including the number of beads visited per male, bead approaches over time, the number of times a male switched between any two different beads, and the fraction of time spent per bead or with the female were calculated from positional data in MATLAB. A visit was defined as an individual spending at least 30 s within 3 fly lengths (approximately 9 mm) of a bead or the female. The timing of an approach was defined as the first frame of a visit bout. Bead switches were defined as the visit of any bead different than the previous one. Male unilateral wing extensions (singing) during the approach of a bead or a female were tracked manually using BORIS (v.7.13.9)56.

Assays were performed in 38-mm-diameter, 3-mm-high circular slope-walled Delrin chambers with a central food patch of 21.5 mm diameter. Videos were recorded in 2 × 2 grids using the same recording setup as above. Females were aspirated first, followed by males, and assays commenced after the last fly was loaded for a 40-min recording. Strain-variation assays were restricted to D. melanogaster because of a lack of availability of further D. erecta strains. For heterospecific group assays, four pairs of D. simulans females and males were transferred to the assay chamber first, followed by one D. erecta female and one male. Ppk23-knockout assays were performed by first transferring a D. melanogaster female target to the arena, followed by mouth aspiration of either a wild-type or a D. erecta ppk23-mutant tester male on ACV. In single-bead assays, a hemispherical black plastic bead of approximately 3 mm diameter (Etsy) was placed on the food patch at the centre of the assay chamber first, followed by aspiration of a single fly, after which the assay commenced. Bead assays were recorded for 20 min. The centroid position and orientation of all flies were tracked and manually corrected for identity swaps in FlyTracker. Reproductive behaviours of males were then inferred in MATLAB from their orientation, heading direction and position relative to visual stimuli and other flies in the arena. Specifically, we extracted male approach and tracking of other flies, close-range courtship and copulations. Approach was defined as the directed movement (greater than or equal to 0.8 mm s−1) towards a sedentary object, such as another fly or a plastic bead from within a distance of maximally 4 fly lengths (approximately 12 mm). We scored approach when the male’s orientation was within 60° of the line connecting his and the target’s centre of area, up to a distance of 1.5 fly lengths (4.5 mm), where it had to be within 45°. Courtship was defined as periods during which males were approaching or tracking another fly or were within 1.5 fly lengths (approximately 4.5 mm) of a female with an angle of at least 45° subtending the line connecting the male’s and female’s centroids. We calculated the courtship index as the fraction of time a male was engaged in courtship for the duration of the assay (Courtship index = Time spent courting/Assay length). If a male copulated, courtship index indicates the fraction of time a male was engaged in courtship until copulation. To calculate the visual experience of males in groups in different chemosensory environments, the angular position and width of other flies in the arena on the focal fly’s visual field were calculated in MATLAB on a frame-by-frame basis as previously described57.

All free-behaviour visual virtual reality assays were performed in 38-mm-diameter, 3-mm-high slope-walled chambers made of Delrin, coated with white self-adhesive vinyl paper (Livelynine) to enhance reflectance and increase the contrast of projected shapes. Visual stimuli were directly projected onto the assay chamber surface28 using a DLP LightCrafter 4500 mini projector (Texas Instruments). Tester males were aspirated into the assay chamber and allowed to acclimate for 5 min before visual stimulus projection started, and recording commenced for 5 min using a Basler acA3088-57uc camera with a 8 mm/f 1.8 lens (Edmund Optics) in pylon Viewer (v.6.3.0). If pairs of flies were used, the female was aspirated first, followed by the male, after which the assay commenced and was recorded for 40 min. All videos were recorded at 30 fps. For all but the visual environment replay assays, either 30 μl 2% (w/v) agar perfumed with ACV (20% v/v) or a 30 μl 2% agar-only control was pipetted into the centre of the assay chamber and allowed to solidify before flies were aspirated. To avoid obstructing the visual environment replay, four equidistant 30-µl dots were placed in a square formation at the periphery of the assay chamber.

Males were presented with either a slow dot rotating clockwise at 16 mm s−1 with a 7.5-mm radius from the centre of the assay chamber, a fast dot rotating counterclockwise at 32 mm s−1 with a 15.5-mm radius from the centre of the assay chamber or both simultaneously. Each dot had a diameter of 3 mm. For mating assays, a female target was added and both visual stimuli were presented after the aspiration of the male. The assay commenced for 40 min or until copulation, whichever was first. The positions of the visual stimuli, female and male were tracked using flyTracker, and male visual object tracking behaviour was inferred in MATLAB on the basis of his orientation, heading direction and position relative to the visual stimuli and female. Tracking was defined as the directed movement towards a moving object within the orientation criteria described for approach in free-behaviour small-arena assays above. The data were then used to calculate the tracking index for each male. The tracking index was defined as the fraction of time a male tracked a visual stimulus during the course of an assay (Tracking index = Time spent tracking/Assay length).

The visual environment replay videos were prepared as follows. Individual trajectories tracked and manually corrected with FlyTracker were extracted from one representative recording of a D. erecta group of five males and five females on ACV and one recorded on agar in a small 38-mm arena. The positional centroid information as well as the orientation of each individual were then used to place a black ellipse at each fly’s position with the long axis (length 3 mm) aligned to the orientation for each frame for a total of 5 min recorded at 30 fps. The 5 min were then looped to create a 40-min video for each chemosensory condition. This was done because on ACV, the accumulation of copulating pairs over time changes the visual environment of a group from one dominated by dynamic movement during courtship to a more sedentary one. We thus extracted a representative 5-min block of a group dominated by courtship on ACV. For the agar video, we extracted the 5-min block beginning at the same time point. For the assay, replay of either the agar or ACV visual environment was paired with agar (2% w/v) or agar perfumed with ACV (20% v/v). A female fly and a male fly were aspirated into the arena, and the recording started together with video replay. Male behaviour towards the female was scored manually using BORIS for 40 min or until copulation, whichever came first. Manual tracking was necessary because flies were obscured by the ellipse projections at low contrast at times, which was not detectable by automated software. The behavioural data were then used to calculate the tracking index for each male.

Males (4–5 days old) were briefly (less than 30 s) anaesthetized on CO2 and subsequently tethered to a custom-milled plastic head plate similar to those used in previous studies38,58. Flies were held in place by a string across the cervical connective and fixed to the head plate by both eyes and the back of the thorax using UV-curable glue (Loctite 3106 and Bondic). The string was subsequently removed, and flies were left to recover in a warm, humidified chamber (25 °C, 50–70% humidity) in the dark. Flies were transferred to an air-supported ball of 5 mm (D. erecta) or 6.35 mm (D. melanogaster) diameter after 30 min and left to acclimatize for 45 min.

We adapted a previous hardware design for presenting tethered males with visual stimuli38,59 and extended it to provide odours with temporal precision. The system, described in detail in ref. 38, consists of an aluminium base keeping an air-supplied Styrofoam ball afloat, held in place by a custom 3D-printed holder adapted to fit either the original 6.35-mm ball used for D. melanogaster males or a 5-mm ball for D. erecta males. The conical screen surrounding the ball was kept at the original dimensions (large diameter: approximately 220 mm, small diameter: approximately 40 mm, height: approximately 60 mm) but was cut from holographic rear projection film (Megicolim). The visual stimulus was rear-projected around the male using a DLP 3010 Light Control Evaluation Module (Texas Instruments). A high-contrast circular visual stimulus of approximately 28° diameter mimicking the angular size of a female fly 2 mm from the male was rear-projected onto the screen, moving in a symmetric 150° arc at constant angular velocity (50° sec−1). For odour delivery, we fit Teflon tubing to the setup providing a constant stream of humidified air with low flow volume (0.5 l min−1) towards the male’s head from the front at a 45° angle and approximately 2 mm from the fly to not obstruct the view on the screen. The tubing was 1 cm in diameter, making sure the entire male was engulfed by the stream of air. Pure ACV odour was mixed with water vapour to a concentration of 50% by two digital mass flow controllers and fed into the outlet tubing by switching from pure air using solenoid valves controlled by means of a data acquisition device (MMC 1408 FS). This ensured the air-flow rate was constant throughout the experiment. Acquisition of the male’s positional readout was based on positional tracking of the spherical treadmill using FicTrac (v.2.0), which was combined with the regulation of visual stimulus generation and odour delivery in MATLAB on a single computer.

Each assay lasted 210 s, beginning with a 30-s baseline period followed by the projection of the oscillating visual stimulus for the remaining 180 s. ACV odour was delivered for 60 s beginning 90 s after assay start, exposing the male to 60 s of visual stimulus only before and after odour delivery.

To assess the role of olfaction in the ACV-dependent visual tracking of D. erecta males in the tethered virtual reality assay, we produced a transgenic line mutant for the chemosensory coreceptors Orco and Ir8a deficient in the principal olfactory pathways previously implicated in the detection of ACV volatiles60,61. Double mutants were tethered and assayed as described above.

The tracking index was defined as previously described36 to reflect the fidelity and vigour of the male’s pursuit of the visual target.

Optogenetics experiments were performed by expressing the light activated cation channel CsChrimson in olfactory sensory neurons (Orco-Gal4) or P1 neurons (71G01-Gal4) with flies reared on sugar-yeast food lacking retinal, a cofactor required for channelrhodopsin function. After 5 to 6 days, tester flies were transferred to food containing 400 μM all-trans-retinal for two days before the experiment. Controls were transferred either to a new sugar-yeast food vial or alternatively to food containing retinal when using a genetic control. Genetic control males carried CsChrimson without a Gal4 driver. For optogenetic activation, flies were exposed to light at a wavelength of 625 nm emitted by red LEDs (Cree Xlamp XP-E2). We used three different experimental configurations.

Small 38-mm assay chambers with a central 21.5-mm food patch formed from agar (2% w/v) perfumed with ACV (20% v/v) or an agar control were backlit with blue light. A female, immobilized by decapitation or an inanimate hemispherical bead (diameter 3 mm), was placed at the centre of the arena. After aspiration of the male, assays were run for 6 min, with two 2-min blocks of baseline background illumination interleaved with the delivery of red light pulsing at 5 Hz with a pulse length of 0.1 s for 2 min. For assays with a decapitated female, red light for optogenetic activation was delivered from below the assay chambers using an array of nine high-power LEDs emitting red light at high intensity to penetrate the Delrin resulting in a power of approximately 7 µW mm−2 at the surface. For bead assays, red light was delivered from above using five high-power LEDs. Male behaviour was tracked using FlyTracker. His position, orientation relative to the female and heading direction were used to track courtship behaviour and to calculate the courtship index as described above.

Small 38-mm assay chambers were coated with a white adhesive film to increase reflectance and illuminated from above using a LightCrafter 4500 mini projector (Texas Instruments) set to emit light exclusively through its blue LED channel by switching off the red and green LEDs for background lighting. P1 neurons labelled with 71G01-Gal4 were activated by red light delivered from above using five high-power LEDs. Assays were run for 6 min, with two 2-min blocks of baseline background illumination interleaved with a 2-min delivery of constant red light in addition to the background light. Male behaviour was tracked using flyTracker. His position, orientation relative to the female and heading direction were used to calculate the tracking index. Tracking was defined as the directed movement towards a moving object within the orientation criteria described for approach in free-behaviour small-arena assays above. The data were then used to calculate the tracking index for each male. The tracking index was defined as the fraction of time a male tracked a visual stimulus during the course of an assay (Tracking index = Time spent tracking/Assay length). Population behaviour was summarized by the fraction of males courting across assays over time.

Males used for optogenetics assays were tethered as described above in ‘Tethered virtual reality assays’. Assays lasted 210 s beginning with a 30-s baseline followed by visual stimulus delivery for the remaining 180 s. One 1.5-mm optic fibre (Edmund Optics) was coupled to a high-power red LED (650 nm, LED Engin) mounted on a heat sink (Ohmite) and placed directly above the head of the fly. Orco+ olfactory sensory neurons were activated by pulsing light at 5 Hz with a pulse length of 0.1 s for 60 s after 90 s. Tracking index was calculated as described above.

Males were tethered as described above. After recovery, the plate was filled with saline (108 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 2 mM CaCl2, 8.2 mM MgCl2, 4 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM NaH2PO4, 5 mM trehalose, 10 mM sucrose, 5 mM HEPES, pH 7.5 with osmolarity adjusted to 265 mOsm) covering the fly’s head. The cuticula above the antenna and between the eyes was cut with a 30-gauge needle and removed with forceps without anaesthesia to provide optical access to the central brain. The tracheae covering the top of the brain were removed using forceps, after which flies were transferred to the ball to recover in darkness for 45 min.

Experiments were performed with an Ultima two-photon laser scanning microscope (Bruker Nanosystems) with a Chameleon Ultra II Ti:Sapphire laser. Samples were excited at a wavelength of 920 nm, and emitted fluorescence was detected with a GaAsP photomultiplier tube (Hamamatsu). Images were acquired in Prairie View (v.5.6; Bruker) with a ×40 Olympus water-immersion objective with 0.8 NA. To reduce noise caused by light emitted by the projector during imaging, the red and green LED channels were switched off. In addition, a piece of blue-light filter paper (Rosco) was placed in front of the projector lens. After the male’s resting period on the ball, the objective was lowered over the brain to identify the brain region of interest (ROI). We centred a small ROI yielding an imaging rate of 4–8 Hz. Laser power was kept low to reduce stress on the fly. ROIs were drawn in a single hemisphere, depending on the neural population imaged. For P1 and LC10a imaging, an ROI was drawn in the LPC and AOTu neuropil, respectively, where axonal projections were densest. For fru and dsx imaging, a larger ROI was drawn, encompassing neurites in both the LPC and adjacent AOTu to capture neural activity simultaneously.

For experiments with a moving visual stimulus, experimental parameters and calculation of the tracking index were as described in ‘Tethered virtual reality assays’. For pheromone tapping experiments, a virgin conspecific female (4–8 days old) was mounted on a micromanipulator serving as pheromone stimulus and presented in sets of six touch bouts 30 s apart to allow neural activity to return to baseline between taps. Pheromone and ACV responses in dsx+ neurons in the LPC were assessed in the same ROI for each animal, where the order of presentation of odour and pheromone stimuli was randomized.

Imaging data were postprocessed and analysed using Fiji (v.2.14.0, NIH). For each experimental recording, frames were motion corrected and aligned along the x and y axes by the Template Matching plugin. Residual background noise from the projector was reduced from raw time series using the Despeckle function. Finally, an ROI was drawn across the entire population of interest containing neuropil to extract the average fluorescence. Fluorescence was normalized in MATLAB for each recording using the average fluorescence over the first 30 s of an experiment as baseline (F0). ∆F/F was defined as ∆Fi/F0 = (Fi − F0)/F0, where i denotes the current frame. Because imaging data were collected at a lower frame rate than behavioural data, behavioural data were downsampled using linear interpolation at the imaging time points. Data from pheromone and ACV imaging of Dsx+ neurons were normalized by matching ∆F/F of pheromone responses across species and adjusting odour responses accordingly.

MATLAB was used for statistical analyses and plotting. The Shapiro–Wilk method was used to test normality, and the appropriate parametric/non-parametric statistical test was used. In cases for which several comparisons were made, appropriate post hoc tests were conducted as indicated in Supplementary Table 1. All statistical tests used were two-tailed.

#1321. Juventus boost as Çelik and McKennie close in on returns before Fiorentina trip

Juventus have been given a boost before Sunday’s trip to Fiorentina, with Zeki Çelik and Weston McKennie both returning to partial team training.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the pair took part in some of Friday’s session at the Continassa with the rest of the squad. Juve’s medical staff will monitor them over the next couple of days before deciding whether either can be involved at the Artemio Franchi.

McKennie picked up a muscle problem in last Sunday’s 2-0 win over Napoli and missed Thursday’s 2-1 Europa League victory at AZ Alkmaar. Çelik has been out with a hamstring injury, and was originally expected to be sidelined until after the international break.

Luciano Spalletti’s side are slowly finding their feet after a difficult spell. Back-to-back defeats, at home to Lazio and away at Genoa, put real pressure on the coach. Juve responded by spending two days on retreat at the J Hotel before the Napoli game, and have now won two in a row.

They are seventh in Serie A on 17 points after 10 games, and they’re unbeaten in the Europa League, where they are well placed for a top-eight finish.

Fiorentina picked up only their second league win of the season at Sassuolo on Monday, with Paolo Vanoli’s side winning 4-2.

#1320. Meet Brighton's merry band of unlikely heroes: a midfielder taking tips from Lionel Messi, a twinkle-toed son of a ballerina and the £3m bargain now running the Premier League

Published: 02:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 02:00 EDT, 6 November 2026

Noel Gallagher arrived at the Etihad Stadium at the weekend hoping to witness a repeat of his beloved Manchester City's FA Cup triumph, only to be sent packing to the soundtrack of the High Flying Seagulls.

That has been the story – no, not morning glory – of Brighton's season. Fabian Hurzeler's side sit third and are beginning to build a compelling case as the Premier League's most unexpected title challengers since Leicester City's remarkable triumph a decade ago.

Even Danny Murphy, rarely one for lavish praise, was impressed by what he saw after the City win.

'They are such a smart team and they are an absolute pleasure to watch with the ball,' he said on BBC's Match of the Day. 'They are brave. They find a way. They are tactically very good.

'No worries who they are playing. There's no respect. They were willing to risk losing to win and that is what you want.'

Brighton's squad is packed with a number of unknowns, courtesy of a scouting network that has been unearthing gems from across the globe for years. This time, though, with an energetic, charismatic coach in Hurzeler and a perfect blend of youth and experience, there is a growing sense that all the pieces may be coming together at exactly the right moment.

Here, Daily Mail Sport's football reporter Tara Anson-Walsh takes a look at the players driving Brighton's unlikely title charge and the stories behind how they ended up on the south coast...

Brighton's squad remains packed with a number of unknowns, courtesy of a scouting network that has been unearthing gems from across the globe for years

With an energetic, charismatic coach in Hurzeler and a perfect blend of youth and experience, there is a growing sense that all the pieces may be coming together at the right moment

A central tenet of Brighton's success this season, 24-year-old Verbruggen has six clean sheets in the Premier League, the joint-most alongside Arsenal's David Raya.

The Dutchman began his career with hometown club NAC Breda before moving to Belgium in 2020. Admired by former Seagulls boss Roberto De Zerbi for his ability to play out from the back, 6ft 4in Verbruggen arrived in England in 2023 for £16.3million, a Belgian league record fee for a goalkeeper.

Three years on, the player who grew up idolising Edwin van der Sar is unsurprisingly being mooted by Real Madrid as a potential long-term replacement for Thibaut Courtois, while Bayern Munich and Tottenham also retain an interest.

Verbruggen has six clean sheets in the Premier League, the joint-most alongside David Raya

The twinkle-toed 27-year-old owes his deft feet to his mother, a professional ballerina who travelled the world performing, as well as to a childhood spent playing tennis in the Netherlands.

After a difficult initial transition from the Eredivisie to Turkey in 2018, the arrival of Vitor Pereira at Fenerbahce in 2021 and a move to wing-back proved the catalyst for Kadioglu's rapid rise.

Brighton regarded the Turkey international's versatility as a key asset. Capable of operating at either full-back position or in midfield, he joined for £25m in the summer of 2024 after impressing at the Euros as one of Hurzeler's first defensive signings.

Kadioglu owes his deft feet to his mother, a professional ballerina who travelled the world performing, as well as to a childhood spent playing tennis in the Netherlands

For a 19-year-old, Vuskovic has already seen his fair share of the world, gaining experience in Poland, Belgium and Germany after emerging as one of Croatia's brightest talents at Hajduk Split.

After becoming the youngest-ever player to feature in the Croatian top flight, the then 16-year-old was snapped up by Tottenham in 2023 and sent out immediately on loan to Hamburg when he joined the north London club two years later.

There, Vuskovic enhanced his reputation as a robust defender, aerial threat and aggressive presser. Brighton subsequently opted to break the bank, paying a club-record £50m and offering the promise of first-team football to secure his signature.

Brighton paid a club-record £50m to Tottenham for 19-year-old centre back Vuskovic's services, sealing the deal with the promise of first-team football

Brighton through and through, Dunk joined the club from Wimbledon's academy aged 12 and has gone on to make 531 appearances under nine managers before being rewarded with the captain's armband in 2019.

Born in the city to a father who played non-League football in Sussex, Dunk has been the one constant throughout Brighton's rise from League One to Europe. Unfazed both on and off the pitch, there is a running joke in the Dunk family that he doesn't reply to his text messages for five days.

#1319. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1318. Calò’s agent slams Mancini after Italy snub: ‘I hope meritocracy isn’t dead’

Giacomo Calò’s agent has criticised Roberto Mancini for leaving the Frosinone midfielder out of the Italy squad for the Nations League games against France and Belgium. He warned that the decision risks being “the death of meritocracy”.

According to Vincenzo Pisacane, via TuttoMercatoWeb, who represents the 29-year-old, Calò’s numbers make him the best midfielder in Italy right now, and he can’t understand why the Frosinone playmaker was overlooked.

Mancini named a 31-man squad on Thursday for the games against France at San Siro on 12 November and Belgium in Brussels three days later. He picked ten midfielders, including first call-ups for teenagers Riccardo Cassano of Como and Simone Lontani of Parma, but Calò was not among them.

Calò has been one of the surprises of the season. He spent most of his career in Serie B and Serie C, and in his first top-flight campaign the regista has five league goals, including goals in four games in a row. No player in the division has created more chances. Frosinone, promoted last season thanks largely to his 10 goals and 15 assists, sit sixth in the table, ahead of Juventus and Napoli.

“It was strange not to see him in Roberto Mancini’s squad. I know Mancini, and I know he takes these things into account,” Pisacane told TuttoMercatoWeb. “If he were 34 or 35, I could have understood it, but he’s 29. On numbers, he’s currently the best midfielder in Italy.

“The players Mancini called up are all very strong, but I don’t think any of them have Calò’s numbers at the moment. That’s why it would have been right to call him up. I hope yesterday’s omission isn’t the death of meritocracy and that Giacomo can be called up later if he keeps this up. Otherwise, it means there’s no logic to the national team call-ups.”

Calò’s form could have taken him away from Frosinone in the summer, but Pisacane revealed that both the player and the club rejected an approach from Sampdoria.

“There was very strong interest from Sampdoria at one point, but Calò always wanted to stay, and the club itself stood in the way and tied him down,” he said.

“I can say that a lot of Serie A clubs I had called before have got back in touch to tell me, ‘What a mistake I made not listening to you.’ That’s already important. There will be time to talk about the market and the future, but right now Giacomo is 100% focused on Frosinone.”

Pisacane also credited coach Massimiliano Alvini, who previously worked with Calò at Cosenza and pushed for his signing.

“His relationship with Alvini is wonderful. Both he and director Castagnini really wanted him last year and did everything to sign him, and he’s fully repaying that trust,” he said. “For me, Alvini has achieved far too little compared to what he could have.”

“Giacomo is calm, though, and even more focused and motivated for the game against Cagliari.”

#1317. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.

#1316. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Numerical simulations for a 1D chain of N = 16 atoms with periodic boundary conditions and Rb/a = 1.4. a,b. Simulations including the full experimentally relevant noise model. a. Time evolution of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) at Δ/Ω = 0.2 and 3.7. Solid curves show noisy numerics including readout confusion; shaded regions indicate the total 1σ uncertainty obtained by combining trajectory and shot-noise errors in quadrature. Noiseless numerics and experimental data are shown for comparison. b. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning, averaged over 0≤t≤4 μs; shading indicates the corresponding total 1σ uncertainty. The noisy numerics use the Aquila-relevant noise model of Extended Data Table 1, with 20 stochastic trajectories, 120 shots per time point, and a sampling interval of 0.01 μs. c,d. Simulations including only positional atom disorder. c. Increase of the resonance peak width near Δ/Ω ≈ 3.7, relative to the zero-disorder case, as a function of the positional disorder strength σp, extracted from Lorentzian fits, together with a simple classical estimate. d. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning for several values of σp. Increasing positional disorder selectively broadens and smooths the resonance peaks, while leaving the rest of the long-time response comparatively unchanged under experimentally relevant noise.

Experimental results for 180 atoms on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. a. The time-averaged expectation values of several k-island observables, namely the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable for k = 1, 2, 3, over time intervals with (top) different initial times ti and fixed final time tf = 4.0 μs, and (bottom) fixed initial time ti = 0.8 μs and different final times tf. The grey dashed vertical lines mark the quench parameters of the time series in panel b, namely the peaks of each island operator (Δ/Ω = 0.0, 1.2, 3.6, 4.8) and the point close to the right exit of the xy 1-island operator region (Δ/Ω = 2.0). b. The time evolution of the expectation values of the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable with k = 1, 2, 3. The drawing on the right shows an example of island conversion processes possible in the 2D system (equivalent to the 1D island conversion Hamiltonian discussed in the Supplementary Information). The arrows in the panels indicate the time series segments for the main resonance at Δ/Ω = 3.6 that tentatively reveal island conversion dynamics: two-islands are rapidly created and then slowly converted into a mix of one- and three-islands. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The time-averaged expectation values of the island operator sum on the cut Rb/a = 1.4 for 16 atoms, and the thermal expectation values of the observable for the effective temperature of the quench using the nearest-neighbor blockade subspace (thermal xy blockade) and the full Hilbert space (thermal full). b. The dependence of the time-averaged blockade violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(1)}\) (also shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a) on V1/Ω at representative constant detuning cuts for 144 atoms. To normalize the blockade violation density to the connectivity and boundary conditions, we scale it by N/NB, where NB = 2NxNy − Nx − Ny is the number of nearest-neighbor bonds. The states along these cuts are prethermal, and thus over a fixed time interval the time averages after peak exhibit exponential scaling [equation (22)], as evidenced by the dashed lines showing fits \(\propto {e}^{-c({V}_{1}/\varOmega )}\). As shown in the Supplementary Information, the upward curvature observed in the experiments relative to the clean exponential scalings at large V1/Ω can be explained by the position disorder, while the calibrated readout errors set the final saturation floor. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The dependence of Δc/Ω (as extracted from \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{L}^{(1)}\rangle }\) using the procedure described in Methods) on inverse linear system size for Rb/a = 1.4 cut. The classical prediction, given by Δc/V2 = 2 − 2(1/Nx + 1/Ny) + 2/(NxNy), is shown for comparison. b. The dependence of the conjugate variable jump ratio (\({\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}\rangle }/{\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}{\hat{n}}_{\langle \langle i\rangle \rangle }\rangle }\)) on the inverse linear system size. The jump ratio is used to probe the Clausius-Clapeyron relation at the DPT. Both the transition point and the jump ratio converge as the system size increases, consistent with a first-order transition. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting statistical and fitting uncertainties as described in Methods.

The classical spin dynamics model is described in the Supplementary Information, where the 2D square lattice has coordination numbers z1 = z2 = z3 = 4. a. Dynamical phase diagram in terms of the long-time averages of the (squared) spin component \({S}_{z}^{2}\). Panels b,c show the three (squared) spin components on b. the cut Rb/a = 1.4 across the phase transition and c. the cut Rb/a = 0.7 across the crossover, each indicated by a grey dashed horizontal line in panel a. The black dashed lines in panels a,b show the phase transition from the approximate analytic solution of the Stoner-Wohlfarth model.

Experimental phase diagrams extended down to Rb/a = 1.0 for 144 atoms. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the Rydberg density observable \({\hat{O}}_{n}\) and the k-neighbor correlation observables \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2 (defined in the main text). Besides the crossover, at low Rb and Δ ≈ 2V1 we observe another distinct dynamical regime, which corresponds to antiblockade dynamics73 characterized by expanding excitation loops74. b. The time-averaged expectation values of the xyk-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3 (equation (4) and surrounding text). The atom schematics in the upper corners show the types and sizes of Rydberg excitations that the observables measure. The grey horizontal line indicates the lower bound Rb/a = 1.2 of the phase diagrams for 180 atoms shown in Fig. 4a. The first-order DPT smooths to a crossover at low Rb, in analogy with the classical Stoner-Wohlfarth scenario (Extended Data Fig. 5). The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

The lattices are shown for Rb/a = 1.4. 1D lattice with a. 52 atoms; and b. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 2 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. 2D square lattice with c. 180 atoms; and d. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 6 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. e. Pulse sequences. (Top) The Rabi frequency Ω is set to a constant value Ω/2π = 2.5 MHz. (Bottom) The detuning Δ is set in the range Δ/Ω ∈ [−4.0, 6.0], and shown here for Δ/Ω = 0.4.

Experimental results on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. Panels a-c show experiments with (left) N = 52 atoms and (right) N = 16 atoms. The geometries are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) observables and the k-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3. Experimental \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) data is equivalent to Fig. 3b. b. The time evolution of the expectation value of the 1-island observable for several values of Δ/Ω on the right exit from the central region, shown as dotted vertical lines in a. c. The time-average \(\bar{p}(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega )=\frac{1}{T}{\sum }_{i}p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,{t}_{i})\) of the Hamming weight probability distribution \(p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,t)={\rm{Tr}}\,(\rho (t){\hat{P}}_{\alpha })\). Projectors \({\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\) arise from the spectral decomposition of the (unnormalized) Hamming weight operator \({\hat{Q}}_{n}\equiv N{\hat{O}}_{n}={\sum }_{\alpha }{\lambda }_{\alpha }{\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\), where λα = 0, …, N denote the possible Hamming weights. The time average is equivalent to marginalization over ti with p(ti) = 1/T. The grey dashed vertical lines identify the distribution at Δ/Ω = 0. d. The mean and variance of the time-averaged Hamming weight probability distribution at Δ/Ω = 0, measured in experiments with different system sizes N. The data are linear, with fits yielding the slope of ~0.275 ± 0.002 for the mean and ~0.106 ± 0.006 for the variance, shown respectively by the red and green solid lines. The approximate scalings are 1/4 and 1/8, shown respectively by the red and green dashed lines, consistent with a state that ergodically explores the blockade subspace. e. The time-averaged Hamming weight probability from numerical simulations with 16 atoms. The experimental data shown are derived from 120 samples per time evolution for 52 atom experiments and 100 samples per time evolution for 16 atom experiments, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

Numerical studies of multiple observables, scaling, and averaging for the 1D chain in a circular geometry on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. The time-averaged expectation values are computed as \(\overline{\langle \hat{O}\rangle }=\frac{1}{{t}_{f}}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{f}}{\rm{d}}t\langle \hat{O}(t)\rangle \). a. The time averages of the blockade-violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) operator, the diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\) operator (also presented in the main text Fig. 2d), and the off-diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) operator. The \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) response vanishes at the main peak, but captures the resonances, suggesting their origin from blockade violations; the \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) response showcases non-analyticities at points where the dynamics is expected to change abruptly. b. The time averages for different system sizes N = 10, …, 20 and final time tf = 10 μs. The curves are nearly identical, indicating a weak system size dependence. c. The time averages for N = 16 atoms and different final times tf. The curves rapidly converge in tf ≈ 0.5 μs. The dashed line denotes the curve for tf = 100 μs, which is the longest time examined in the numerics, while the squares denote the diagonal ensemble averages, which are equal to the time averages in the strictly infinite-time limit. d. The time averages of the blockade-violation operator for N = 16 atoms and different quench parameters Δ/Ω, reflecting the 1D experiments in Fig. 3a. Similar to the experimental results, the curves show exponential decay, corroborating prethermal dynamics even at small system sizes.

Numerical results obtained using the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) method for a chain of N = 52 Rydberg atoms with open boundary conditions. The blockade radius is Rb/a = 1.4. The system is evolved up to \({t}_{\max }=4.0\,\mu {\rm{s}}\) with a time step Δt = 0.01 μs, and the Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, with longer-range terms truncated. a. Real-time dynamics of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) for two representative detunings, (top) Δ/Ω = 0.0 and (bottom) Δ/Ω = 0.5, illustrating convergence of the oscillatory behavior with increasing maximum MPS bond dimension \({\chi }_{\max }\). b. Time-averaged value \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle }\) as a function of detuning Δ/Ω, where the plotted values are averaged over the final 2.0 μs of the evolution. The curves correspond to different maximum bond dimensions \({\chi }_{\max }\). Both the real-time dynamics and the time-averaged observables exhibit rapid convergence as \({\chi }_{\max }\) increases, with \({\chi }_{\max }\gtrsim 256\) yielding nearly indistinguishable results, indicating that the dynamics are well converged with respect to entanglement truncation at the probed times.

#1315. Milan target defensive reinforcements with Inácio top of the list

Milan are preparing to strengthen their defence when the transfer window opens in January, and Sporting CP captain Gonçalo Inácio remains their first choice.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the Rossoneri see a new centre-back as a priority with less than two months until the market reopens. Inácio is still top of the list, but a deal will be difficult because of Sporting’s high valuation. Milan will try anyway, hoping the Portuguese club can be persuaded to negotiate.

The 25-year-old knows Ruben Amorim well, having played under the Milan coach for several seasons at Sporting. He reportedly has a €60m release clause, although Portuguese outlet A Bola suggest a fee of €40-45m could be enough to sign him.

Inácio isn’t the only name on the list. Milan are also considering investing in younger players, and they are big admirers of Borussia Dortmund’s Luca Reggiani. The 2008-born Italian left Sassuolo’s academy for Germany at 16 and made his Bundesliga and Champions League debuts last season.

Union Saint-Gilloise’s Massiré Sylla is another option. The 21-year-old Senegalese defender joined the Belgian club from Norwegian side Lyn in January, after being named Young Player of the Year in Norway’s second tier.
